title: Chapter 72 – The Pill Hall
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The Pill Hall smells of smoke, bitter bark and boiled plums, and Jian has come to like all three.

It stands on the second terrace above the Hundred Stairs, a long low building with a stone chimney at each end and a courtyard of packed earth between its two wings. Furnaces line the courtyard in rows, clay kettles on iron legs, each with a numbered tin tag. Beyond the courtyard lies the herb store, with its racks of dried roots and its sleepy guard. Beyond the store, behind a plain door that nobody uses, lies Elder Bai's furnace room.

Jian is standing at that door at dawn, three days after the Contribution Hall, with a clean tunic and a sealed chit in his hand.

The chit came from Steward Gu that morning, folded small, with the Elder's plum-colored seal pressed into the wax. It says only: Apprentice interview. Furnace room. Do not be late and do not bring food.

He knocks.

"It is open," says a voice from inside, thick with plum.

The furnace room is round, with a domed ceiling blackened by a century of smoke. A single great furnace of bronze stands in the center on a stone ring, as tall as Jian's chest, with a bowl-shaped mouth and three small vents. Around it, on shelves, hang a hundred little jars, each labeled in a different hand. Elder Bai sits on a low stool beside the bronze, with his sleeves rolled to the elbow and a bowl in his lap.

He does not stand. He gestures at a second stool across the furnace, so that the bronze lies between them.

"Sit. Not close. The fire is banked, but it has opinions."

Jian sits.

"I have taken no apprentice in nineteen years," says Bai, in the voice of a man mentioning the weather. "The last one is now a Grand Elder's cook. I did not like what the Sect did to him, and I did not like what I did to him either." He eats a plum. "You will understand if I ask you a number of rude questions."

"Yes, Elder."

"How old are you?"

"Ten."

"How long have you been at the furnace?"

"Eleven days, Elder."

"Who taught you?"

"Steward Gu showed me the Level 1 forms. The Hall's scroll did the rest."

"And the idea about the salt?"

"The first batch cracked."

"So you said." Bai chews. "Do you know what I think, Lin Jian? I think it is not a very good answer. I think the true answer is that you looked at the crack and saw something in it, and I think you have a habit of looking at things in that way, and I think you do not wish to say so."

Jian does not move. In the Interface, nothing stirs. He has not spent a breath of cultivation energy in this room, and he does not mean to.

"Elder, I do not know what I see. I know what I count."

"Mm." Bai tilts his round head. "That is almost an answer. Almost is better than a lie." He sets down the bowl. "Give me your hand."

* * *

It is a Foundation alchemist's examination, and it is very quick.

Bai takes Jian's wrist in two thick fingers and holds it. His thumb lies on the inside of the forearm, a little below the joint, and a faint warmth spreads through the skin, not Qi, exactly, but the pressure of someone listening. Jian keeps his breathing even. The Seasons Veil turns its false slow wheel under his ribs, and he has the strange, exact, uncomfortable impression of a very patient man leaning an ear against a door.

"Hm," says the Elder. "Ninth layer."

"Yes."

"Peak." A pause. "Rare, for ten. Rarer for five roots." He lets go. "I have been told. I did not believe it. You carry yourself like a boy of the third layer, you know. You wear the slow wheel well. A trick of the old hiding schools. Someone good taught you."

Jian lifts his eyes. Bai only chews.

"I will not report what I felt," says Bai. "I would like it understood that I could. The Mirror in the Register hall reads what is shown to it. I read what is held." He picks up a second plum. "Why do you wish to be an alchemist?"

"Because I need pills, Elder."

It is out before he can polish it. Bai looks at him for a moment, and then, to Jian's surprise, he laughs, a short rich bark.

"Honest. Good." The plum goes into his mouth. "Most of them say to serve the Sect. They are lying, and so am I, when I say I took the position for the sake of the pills." He swallows. "It is the right reason. The pill is the thing. Everything else is a hall."

* * *

The trial month is a plain arrangement. Bai explains it in six sentences, between plums.

Jian will report to the Pill Hall at dawn on six days of seven. He will sweep, wash, haul water and fetch reagents for Steward Gu until noon. After noon, if the work is done, he may light a furnace. He will keep a log of every batch, good or bad, in his own hand. Every failure costs the Hall its reagents and must be paid back in low stones or in points. At the end of thirty days, Elder Bai will decide whether the boy stays.

"If I decide against," says Bai, "you keep your eighty points and your methods, and you go back to the terraces. If I decide for, you become what the Sect calls an apprentice of the Pill Hall, which means you are fed, housed, and not much liked." He shrugs. "I have no further promises."

"And a Master, Elder?"

The round face does not change. "I did not say Master. I said apprentice. A Master teaches. An apprentice learns what is left on the table." A small crooked smile. "If I wished to teach you, I would need an Elder's seal, a book of obligations, and a great deal of paper. I do not wish to. Not yet."

Not yet. Jian files it.

"Today," says Bai, rising, "we shall see whether you are worth the stones. Come."

* * *

The test is the Marrow Wash.

It is the second of the three Level 1 pills the Hall teaches to the Outer Court. Breath-Gathering is for Qi. Blood Seal is for wounds. The Marrow Wash is for the bone: a bitter green pill, low tier, that scours impurities from the marrow and leaves a disciple's body ready for more of the same. Every outer disciple who hopes for the third stage will take twelve over the course of a year. The Hall sells them for five points.

Making them is harder than taking them.

"Six herbs," says Bai, standing at the long bench in the main courtyard, with a row of jars before him. "Marrow vine root, one finger. Frostbell, crushed. Heartroot, a pinch of the lowest grade. Cinnabar grit, so fine that it floats. Mourner's cup, the dried petal. And bone ash of a black goat, which is the ugly part." He steps aside. "Make me one pill."

"One, Elder?"

"One that works." Bai folds his arms. "I will tell you now that most of the Hall's apprentices need nine or ten tries. The Level 1 formulas are not difficult. The fire is."

Jian looks at the furnace.

It is a standard apprentice's kettle, tin tag 14. Charcoal sits in the base, a bellows leans against the leg, and a clay lid with a single small vent waits on the bench. There is nothing remarkable in it, and he sees at once what the matter is.

The fire is not a thing that sits still.

A pill is not cooked. It is persuaded. Each herb gives up its essence at a different temperature, in a different order, and the whole skill of an alchemist is to bring the kettle up to that heat, hold it, bring it up again, without a single flash or dip. The Hall teaches this with a sand clock and a count of breaths. Boil for sixty. Raise the heat. Lid on for a hundred.

The count is a crutch.

He feels it clearly as he lights the charcoal. Not the number. The color. A flame is not one thing; it carries inside it a slow gradient from red to white, and the white is hotter and the red is gentler, and for a boy with a fire root in his five, that gradient is as plain as the grain in a plank.

He has not noticed it before. He has not needed to.

He weighs the herbs. He grinds them in the order the scroll dictates. He puts the vine root in first, on a low flame, the red of a dying coal, and counts sixty breaths, and the Elder watches without a word.

At the end of the count the vine root is gray.

It should be brown.

Too cool.

He knew. He knew it as soon as it was done, and he stands there, with his hand over the vent and the small bitter smell of an under-cooked root in his nose, while Bai says nothing at all.

"Start again," says the Elder. "The reagents are yours to pay."

* * *

The first batch is a failure, and so is the second.

The first is too cool and the second too hot; the herbs, which should have melted into one another, form instead a gummy black ball that sticks to the lid and has to be chipped out with a spatula. Jian cleans the kettle, wipes the lid, weighs again. He does not complain. He does not look at the Elder, who has gone to sit under the eave with a bowl of plums.

On the third, he tries to cheat.

It is not much of a cheat. He knows what the flame ought to look like; he has watched it twice. He brings the heat up to the exact shade of orange the scroll implies, holds it, adds the frostbell, lids the kettle for a hundred breaths. The smell is right. The color through the vent is right. He lifts the lid.

The pill is perfectly formed, round, green, glossy. It also contains a faint, very faint, fracture line down one side, the kind of flaw that can be found only by someone who is looking for it.

He knows it is there because he looks.

He does not call for the Elder. He picks up the pill, and cracks it in two with his thumbs. Inside the green shell, the core is gray and powdery.

"Three," says Bai, from the shade.

"Yes, Elder."

"Sixty low stones."

It is not a rebuke. It is the price: six herbs, three batches, each with a handful of the cheaper reagents and a pinch of the dearer, and the bone ash. Jian has the stones. Wenyuan sewed them into his hem, forty and two, and he has been spending them in ones and twos since the Register. He counts the sixty now into the steward's palm. It takes everything in the hem and eighteen more from the purse Hu gave him, and when he is done, there is nothing left in either.

The steward weighs them on his small balance, because he is a careful man.

"Correct," he says to his hands.

Jian says nothing. In his head the number turns over: Zero. Zero in the hem, and nothing in the purse. I have eighty points and no stones. It is the first time since the Garden that he has owned nothing at all.

He looks again at the furnace.

* * *

The fourth batch he does without the count.

He does not decide to. He is lighting the charcoal again, with a steadiness that surprises him, and the flame comes up through the red, and there is a moment where the heat in the kettle and the heat in his own chest seem to match, a slight, strange, dizzy sense of agreement. The Five Seasons Seal turns once, softly, below the navel. It is not Qi. He does not draw on it. It is more as though the flame were looking back.

He adds the vine root.

He watches the color of the fire along the lip of the kettle. When the red goes to amber, he waits. When the amber begins to pale at the edge, he waits. Then, at a shade he could not name, he lifts the root out with the tongs and sets it on the stone.

It is brown.

He does the same with the frostbell, and the cinnabar, and the Heartroot, and the petal. He does not count. He watches the flame, and at each change he moves, and the time between the changes is not the same. The Hall's scroll says sixty. It is fifty-one. The scroll says a hundred. It is a hundred and thirty, because the cinnabar needs a long slow soak.

When the ash goes in last, off the heat, he is aware that Bai has stopped eating.

He lifts the lid.

The pill sits at the bottom of the kettle, small and green and perfectly round. It has no fracture line. It has a faint ring of paler green at the edge, like the ring on his Breath-Gathering, and when he turns it with the tongs it catches the light like a bead of jade.

He sets it in a dish.

Bai has risen from his bench. He crosses the courtyard in six slow strides, and takes up the pill, and holds it to the light. Then he bites it, in half, in the same unceremonious way as before, and chews.

He does not spit.

"Tier low," he says slowly. "Quality... medium." He swallows. "Fourth try. No count." The small pale eyes come up. "Do you know that you did not count?"

"Yes, Elder."

"Do you know that the scroll says sixty?"

"It was fifty-one, Elder. The root was done at fifty-one."

"How did you know?"

Jian has had an answer ready since the second batch. He gives it. "The flame told me."

"The flame."

"The color changes, Elder. At the edge of the kettle. The Hall's count is for a fire that burns at the same rate every time. Mine did not."

Bai is quiet.

"I have taught alchemy for ninety years," he says at last. "I have watched seven hundred apprentices burn their first batches. Four of them could read fire." He turns the half-pill over in his fingers. "Three were killed in the war. The fourth is a Grand Elder, and I do not speak to her." A pause. "It is not a skill the Sect teaches, Lin Jian. It is a skill the Sect is afraid of. You see why?"

"No, Elder."

"Because a boy who reads fire does not need a Master."

The courtyard is silent. Overhead, the bell on the Contribution Hall tolls the third hour, and a servant on the far side drops a bucket and swears.

"I will take you," says Bai. "As apprentice. Not as Master. Not yet." He wipes his thumb on his robe. "You will show no one what you did today. You will count aloud, if anyone is watching. You will count wrong, if they are not looking closely." A dry smile. "It is easy to count wrong. It takes a little practice."

"Yes, Elder."

"And you will pay for your own failures. Sixty stones. I will not forgive them." He crooks a finger. "I will lend you the next ones."

Cost.

Jian bows. The pill, he notices, is gone from the dish. Bai has swallowed it.

* * *

"The legacy," says Bai, "is a very ordinary thing."

They are sitting in the shade of the eave, on the bench where the Elder keeps his plums. It is past noon. The furnaces are lit down the length of the courtyard, and a line of boys in gray stand over them, counting under their breaths. A stray cat crosses the yard with a dead mouse.

"Every Hall in the Sect keeps a legacy," Bai continues. "Not a pill. A body of pills. Recipes, forms, fires, tricks, the whole slow knowledge of what the Hall has learned in a thousand years. It is divided by Rank. Rank 1 is open. Any outer disciple with a leave may study Level 1 pills at the Hall's scroll. That is what you have been reading."

"And Rank 2?"

"Rank 2 is the second floor of the Library." The Elder cracks a plum stone between his teeth. "It is sealed. It is available to a disciple who has earned two hundred points and holds an Elder's permission, signed and sealed in the Library's book. The permission names the legacy. It names the reason. If the reason is poor, the permission is refused."

"Two hundred."

"Yes."

"I have eighty."

"You have eighty and no stones, and a trial month." Bai says it kindly. "I suggest you earn the rest."

Jian looks at the courtyard.

"Rank 3 is the third floor, and you do not need to know about that," says Bai. "Rank 4 and above is in the Elders' own libraries, and each Elder holds a piece. The Sect is built, you will notice, so that no one person can read the whole of anything." He lifts his eyebrows. "A cautious design. I was not consulted."

"Elder." Jian chooses his words. "The Foundation Establishment pill is a Level 2. Is it in the Rank 2 legacy?"

The Elder's hand stops with a plum halfway to his mouth.

It is a very small stop. The plum does not fall. The smile does not change. But Jian, who has spent the past ten days learning to read the small pauses of men who are good at hiding, feels the shift as plainly as a draft.

"What makes you ask?"

"My brother Feng is trying for it. He is at the ninth layer. He has been told it costs six hundred points."

"Ah." The plum goes into the Elder's mouth. "Your brother. Yes." A pause. "It does cost six hundred. And there is a public formula for it. You may read it at the Hall's scroll, if you like. It is on the last page."

* * *

The scroll is a long roll of yellow paper in a glass case at the end of the herb store, held open by two brass weights.

Jian has seen it twice. He has read the first three pages: the three Level 1 pills in neat columns, the herbs, the fires, the quirks. He has not read the last page. It has no entry on it for any outer disciple. It has a single line, at the top, in the faded red ink of a very old hand.

Foundation Establishment Pill (Level 2). Reagents: Earthheart root, one; Azure dew, three drops; pale jade powder, one liang; sun-forged cinnabar, two grains. Fire: steady, middle, one night. Method: refer to the Master of the Hall.

That is all.

He reads it twice. The case is locked. He is at an angle where his body blocks the view from the courtyard, and he is careful to keep his hands at his sides. He does not want to be seen copying.

Four reagents.

The ink is faded but legible. The method line is blank. The text breaks off, in the old red hand, mid-sentence, and the glass over the break is a little duller than the rest, as though someone had once rubbed at it, thoughtfully, with a thumb.

The recipe is incomplete.

He is no alchemist. But he has been reading Level 1 forms for eleven days, and every one of them has been a closed loop: herbs, fire, method, yield. A pill with four reagents and no stated method is not a formula. It is a list of ingredients and a warning.

Behind him the gravel crunches.

"It is a famous scroll," says Bai.

Jian does not turn at once. He lets his breath out slowly and lowers his eyes to the glass. "It has no method."

"No." The Elder has come up on his left, soft-footed for so round a man. "It was cut. A very long time ago." He rests a finger on the case, beside the dull patch. "Do you know how many apprentices have tried to make a Foundation Establishment pill from the four reagents?"

"No, Elder."

"Forty-one. In my time." The mild voice is entirely level. "Thirty-nine failed. The pill is a lump of ash. Two succeeded, after a fashion, and produced a thing that made a Foundation Establishment attempt survivable, one time in four." He taps the glass. "That is the public pill. It is the pill that sits on the shelf at six hundred points. I have made it myself, nineteen times. It is not the one the Founders made."

"There was a true one?"

"There was a true one." Bai takes his finger from the case. "I should not say so. I am saying so. You may consider it a thing an old man told a boy over a plum." He looks at Jian, gravely. "Do you understand why I tell you?"

"No, Elder."

"Nor do I." The pale eyes crease. "Come. I would like to show you something."

* * *

The sealed shelf is at the back of the furnace room, behind the bronze.

It is a small alcove, cut into the stone of the wall, with an arch of black iron and a door of plain gray wood. The door has no handle. It has a seal, a plum-colored seal, pressed into a disk of wax across the join. Bai breaks it with his thumbnail and the door swings inward.

Inside, on a shelf of white jade, a single box sits alone.

It is a box of dark red lacquer, with a lid inlaid in silver thread. It is the length of a man's hand. Bai lifts it down with both palms, as if it were a sleeping bird, and sets it on the furnace's stone ring. Then he opens the lid.

Jian sees the pill.

It lies on a bed of black silk, round, pale gold, no larger than a hazelnut. It does not shine. It sits, quiet in the lamplight, with a light of its own that has nothing to do with the lamp. A faint, slow pulse moves through it, once every few breaths, like a thing remembering how to breathe. He feels it in his teeth. He feels it, strangely, in the Seal beneath his navel, and a quiet low note rings through him, from the soles of his feet to the roots of his hair.

He keeps his face blank. He has had a great deal of practice.

"A real one," says Bai softly. "Level 2. Peak quality. Made by the Founders' own hand, six hundred years ago, for a disciple who died before he could take it." He closes the lid half-way, so that only a thread of gold shows at the edge. "I have kept it for fifty-two years. I do not know why."

"Elder."

"Yes?"

"Why show me?"

For a long moment the Elder does not answer. He stands with his thick hands on the lacquer, his round pink face lit from below, the plum stone, for once, absent from his mouth. He looks like a man who has opened a door in his house he has not opened in a very long time, and does not know what will come out of it.

"Because you will want to look at it again," he says, "and I would rather you looked in my presence than in my absence."

He says it quite gently, and Jian, who has been hunted by Blood Shadow hunters and cornered by Deacons and has not, in the last month, been frightened by any of them, feels the back of his neck turn cold.
